publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
2,3-Dimethyl-2-butene can be prepared by heating which of the following compounds with a strong acid?
  1. (CH3)2C=CH-CH2-CH3
  2. (CH3)2CH-CH2-CH=CH2
  3. drawn by the pipeline traced from the booklet's printed picture, its SMILES checked · C7H14 name ✓
    (CH3)2CH-CH(CH3)-CH=CH2
  4. (CH3)3C-CH=CH2
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)

    → the working concludes: option 4

    printed solution, as in the booklet
    Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
    1. The target (CH3)2C=C(CH3)2 has 6 carbons with a C4 chain carrying two methyls; option 3 has 7 carbons and options 1 and 2 have unbranched skeletons that cannot give it without a rearrangement of the right type.
    2. Protonation of option 4 by Markovnikov addition: (CH3)3C-CH=CH2 + H+ → (CH3)3C-+CH-CH3 (secondary carbocation).
    3. A 1,2-methyl shift gives the more stable tertiary carbocation: (CH3)3C-+CH-CH3 → (CH3)2+C-CH(CH3)2.
    4. Loss of H+ from the adjacent C–H gives the most substituted alkene: (CH3)2+C-CH(CH3)2 → (CH3)2C=C(CH3)2, i.e. 2,3-dimethyl-2-butene, which is option 4.
    printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
    44 highagree
    difficultyhard · 4 steps
    stepsDraw the target 2,3-dimethyl-2-butene, (CH3)2C=C(CH3)2, and compare its six-carbon skeleton with each option's skeleton (option 3 has seven carbons; options 1 and 2 have a 2-methylpentane skeleton that hydride shifts cannot change) → Protonate the remaining candidate alkene, (CH3)3C-CH=CH2, by Markovnikov addition to give the secondary carbocation next to the tert-butyl group → Recognise the 1,2-methyl shift that turns the secondary carbocation into the more stable tertiary carbocation, which changes the carbon skeleton to the target's → Lose H+ from the adjacent carbon (Saytzeff) to give the tetrasubstituted alkene and confirm it is the target
    whyThe candidate has to carry an alkene through protonation, a skeleton-changing 1,2-methyl shift and elimination, and must rule out the other options by comparing carbon skeletons.
    the catchNo option has the target's carbon skeleton, so the candidate must see that a carbocation methyl shift is needed. Options 1 and 2 have the right carbon count and only rearrange by hydride shifts, so they look plausible but give a 2-methylpentene skeleton.

    READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
    The formation of the oxide ion, O2-(g), from oxygen atom requires first an exothermic and then an endothermic step as shown in below:
    O(g) + e- ⟶ O-(g) ; ΔfH⊖ = -141 kJ mol-1
    O-(g) + e- ⟶ O2-(g) ; ΔfH⊖ = +780 kJ mol-1
    Thus process of formation of O2- in gas phase is unfavourable though O2- is isoelectronic with neon. It is due to the fact that,
    1. Oxygen is more electronegative.
    2. Addition of electron in oxygen results in larger size of the ion.
    3. Electron repulsion outweighs the stability gained by achieving noble gas configuration.
    4. O- ion has comparatively smaller size than oxygen atom.
    The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)

        READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
        On heating which of the following releases CO2 most easily?
        1. MgCO3
        2. CaCO3
        3. K2CO3
        4. Na2CO3
        The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
        1. Thermal stability order
        2. K2CO3 > Na2CO3 > CaCO3 > MgCO3
        3. Therefore MgCO3 releases CO2 most easily.
        4. MgCO3 Δ  MgO + CO2

        → the working concludes: option 1

        printed solution, as in the booklet
        Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
        1. Alkali metal carbonates (Na2CO3, K2CO3) are thermally very stable and do not readily lose CO2 on heating.
        2. Group 2 carbonates decompose as MCO3 → MO + CO2, and their stability increases down the group as cation size increases and polarising power falls.
        3. Mg2+ is the smallest, most polarising cation, so the order of stability is MgCO3 < CaCO3 < Na2CO3 < K2CO3.
        4. The least stable carbonate, MgCO3, releases CO2 most easily, which is option 1.

            subtopic 1Colour Blindness

            printed in the booklet

            READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
            A colour blind man marries a woman with normal sight who has no history of colour blindness in her family. What is the probability of their grandson being colour blind?
            1. 0.25
            2. 0.5
            3. 1
            4. Nil
            The publisher's solutionprinted answer (2)
            1. Father (Colourblind)
            2. ↓ Daughter (Carrier)
            3. ↓ Grandson [50% Probability (0.5)]

            → the working concludes: option 2

            printed solution, as in the booklet
            Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · medium
            1. Colour blindness is X-linked recessive: man is XcY, woman with no family history is XX.
            2. Their children: daughters XcX (carriers), sons XY (normal).
            3. A grandson through a carrier daughter (married to a normal man XY) is colour blind with probability 12.
            4. A grandson through a normal son receives no Xc, so probability 0.
            5. Taking either line equally likely: 12×12 + 12× 0 = 0.25, which is option 1.
            printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
            21 mediumsolved differs from official
            difficultyhard · 4 steps
            stepsRecall that colour blindness is X-linked recessive (man is XcY, woman with no family history is XX homozygous normal) → Cross the parents: all daughters are carriers (XXc), all sons are normal (XY) → Work out which route can produce an affected grandson: a son passes only Y to his sons (no risk), so it must come through a carrier daughter, assumed to marry a normal man → Cross carrier daughter x normal man and take the proportion among her sons that are XcY
            whyThe work is a two-generation X-linked pedigree: set up the parental cross, identify the carrier daughter as the only route to an affected grandson, then run the second cross and read the ratio among sons rather than among all children.
            the catchThe stem leaves unstated whether the grandson comes through a son or a daughter and whom the daughter marries; the distractors match plausible wrong routes - 'Nil' is the son's-line result and 0.25 is the ratio taken over all grandchildren instead of grandsons.

            solver reasoning: Daughters are all carriers and sons all normal; a grandson via a carrier daughter has 1/2 chance, via a normal son 0, so overall 1/2 x 1/2 = 0.25.

            In the following human pedigree, the filled symbols represent the affected individuals. Identify the type of given pedigree.
            1. X-linked dominant
            2. Autosomal dominant
            3. X-linked recessive
            4. Autosomal recessive
            The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
            1. The given pedigree represents inheritance of Autosomal recessive trait.

            → the working concludes: option 4

            printed solution, as in the booklet
            Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
            1. In generation II, an unaffected man and an unaffected woman have an affected son in III, and in generation III two unaffected parents have two affected sons in IV, so the trait is recessive (dominant traits cannot skip from unaffected parents).
            2. The affected woman in II (XaXa if X-linked recessive) would pass Xa to every son, so all her sons would be affected; her son in III is unaffected, so the trait is not X-linked recessive.
            3. All matings fit autosomal recessive: affected aa father I x carrier Aa mother gives aa and Aa children; carrier Aa × Aa couples give aa affected sons, so the answer is option 4.
            printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
            44 highagree
            difficultyhard · 4 steps
            stepsRead the four-generation pedigree and find unaffected parents (generation III couple) with affected children in generation IV, so the trait skips a generation and is recessive; this rules out both dominant options → Note the sex distribution: an affected female in generation II and affected males in generations I-IV, so the trait is not limited to males → Test X-linked recessive against each affected individual: the affected generation II daughter needs the married-in generation I mother to be a carrier, and the affected generation III son of an unaffected generation II male needs his married-in mother to be a carrier → Reject X-linked recessive because it needs several unrelated married-in carriers, and choose autosomal recessive as the simpler explanation
            whyThe candidate has to trace the pedigree across four generations, use the skipped generation to exclude the dominant modes, then check X-linked recessive person by person and drop it because it needs extra assumptions.
            the catchThe pedigree does not strictly rule out X-linked recessive. The choice between the two recessive options rests on which explanation is more likely, which is a judgement beyond the NCERT rule-based pedigree checks. Most affected individuals are male, which makes the X-linked recessive option a plausible trap.

            subjectPhysics
            chapterElectromagnetic Induction high confidence
            why this chapterThe answer turns on Lenz's law: the magnetic flux through the coil from the moving electron's field first increases then decreases, so the induced current reverses direction as the electron passes.
            subtopic 1Direction of Induced Current
            why this subtopicThe answer depends on finding the direction of the current induced in the coil, which reverses because the flux from the moving electron grows as it approaches and falls as it moves away.
            printed in the booklet
            publisher’s solution, as printed
            READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
            An electron moves on a straight line path XY as shown. The abcd is a coil adjacent to the path of electron. What will be the direction of current, if any, induced in the coil?
            1. No current induced
            2. abcd
            3. adcb
            4. The current will reverse its direction as the electron goes past the coil
            The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
            1. When e- comes closer the induced current will be anticlockwise
            2. When e- comes farther induced current will be clockwise.

            → the working concludes: option 4

            printed solution, as in the booklet
            Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
            1. The electron moves from X to Y, so the equivalent conventional current I flows from Y to X (to the left).
            2. For a leftward current, the field at points above the line is →B ∝ I d→l × ˆr = (-ˆx)×(+ˆy) = -ˆz, i.e. into the page through the coil.
            3. While the electron approaches the coil, ΦB (into the page) increases, so by Lenz's law the induced current makes a field out of the page: anticlockwise, a → b → c → d.
            4. After the electron passes the coil, ΦB decreases, so the induced current makes a field into the page: clockwise, a → d → c → b.
            5. The induced current reverses direction as the electron goes past the coil, which is option 4.
            printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
            44 highagree
            difficultyhard · 4 steps
            stepsConvert the electron's motion X to Y into a conventional current directed Y to X (negative charge) → Apply the right-hand rule to find the direction of the magnetic field of that current in the region above the line where the coil sits (out of or into the plane) → Track how the flux through the coil changes in time: it grows while the electron approaches and falls after it passes the coil → Apply Lenz's law to each phase to get the induced current sense (abcd vs adcb) and see that it changes sign as the electron passes
            whyThe work is a sign conversion for the electron's charge, a right-hand-rule field direction, a time-varying flux argument over the approach and recession of the charge, and Lenz's law applied separately to each phase.
            the catchOptions 2 and 3 are each the correct sense for only one phase of the motion (approach or recession), so a candidate who analyses only one phase, or forgets the electron's negative charge, lands exactly on a distractor; option 1 traps those who think a charge moving past (not towards) a loop causes no flux change.

            Water rises to a height ‘h’ in capillary tube. If the length of capillary tube above the surface of water is made less than ‘h’, then:

            3. Water rises upto the top of capillary tube and stays there without overflowing

            The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)

            → the working concludes: option 3

            Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
            1. Capillary rise obeys h = 2Tcosθrρ g, i.e. hR = 2Tρ g is constant, where R = rcosθ is the meniscus radius.
            2. If the tube length l < h, water rises to the top and the meniscus radius increases to R' = hRl so that lR' = hR.
            3. The meniscus flattens and the water stays at the top without overflowing (no perpetual fountain), which is option 3.

            why this subtopicThe answer rests on the telescope's magnifying power in normal adjustment, f_o/f_e, which equals L/I because the eyepiece images the objective (distance f_o+f_e) with magnification f_e/f_o.
            printed in the booklet
            publisher’s solution, as printed
            READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
            In an astronomical telescope in normal adjustment a straight black line of the length L is drawn on inside part of objective lens. The eye-piece forms a real image of this line. The length of this image is I. The magnification of the telescope is:
            1. LI
            2. LI+1
            3. LI-1
            4. L+IL-I
            The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
            1. Magnification by eyepiece
            2. m = ff+u
            3. -IL = fefe + (-(f0 + fe)
            4. ⇒ IL = fef0
            5. m. p. = f0fe = LI

            → the working concludes: option 1

            printed solution, as in the booklet
            Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
            1. In normal adjustment the objective-eyepiece separation is fo + fe, so the line is at u = -(fo + fe) from the eyepiece.
            2. Lens formula: 1v - 1u = 1fe ⇒ 1v = 1fe - 1fo + fe = fofe (fo + fe).
            3. So v = fe (fo + fe)fo, a real image.
            4. Linear magnification of this image: IL = v|u| = fefo.
            5. Telescope magnification M = fofe = LI, which is option 1.

            Q180Physics
            subjectPhysics
            chapterRay Optics high confidence
            why this chapterThe answer turns on total internal reflection at the prism's 45-degree face: only red (n = 1.39) has a critical angle above 45 degrees and emerges, while green and blue are totally internally reflected, which is ray optics (prism / TIR).
            subtopic 1Total Internal Reflection (TIR)
            why this subtopicThe answer depends on the critical-angle condition for total internal reflection at the 45 degree hypotenuse face (sin C = 1/n, so green and blue with n > 1.414 are totally reflected while red with n = 1.39 emerges).
            printed in the booklet
            publisher’s solution, as printed
            READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
            A beam of light consisting of red, green and blue colours is incident on a right angled prism. The refractive index of the material of the prism for the above red, green and blue wavelengths are 1.39,1.44 and 1.47 respectively. The prism will:
            1. Separate the red colour part from the green and blue colours
            2. Separate the blue colour part from the red and green colours
            3. Separate all the three colours from one another
            4. Not separate the three colours at all
            The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
            1. For TIR I > Ic so Sin i > sin Ic
            2. Sin 45° > 1μ ⇒ μ2 ⇒ μ = 1.414
            3. Since μ of green and violet are greater than 1.414 so they will total internal refrected. But red colour will be vetracted.
            4. So Ans. is (1)

            → the working concludes: option 1

            printed solution, as in the booklet
            Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
            1. The beam is incident normally on face AB, so it enters undeviated.
            2. From the geometry (∠ C = 45°, ∠ B = 90°), the ray meets face AC at an angle of incidence i = 45°.
            3. Total internal reflection at AC requires sin 45° > 1n, i.e. n > 2 ≈ 1.414.
            4. Red: n = 1.39 < 1.414, so red refracts out through AC.
            5. Green: n = 1.44 > 1.414 and blue: n = 1.47 > 1.414, so both are totally internally reflected.
            6. Hence red is separated from green and blue, which is option 1.
            printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
            11 highagree
            difficultymedium · 3 steps
            stepsNote the beam is normal to face AB so it enters undeviated, and from the 45-degree prism geometry it meets face AC at an angle of incidence of 45 degrees → Apply the total internal reflection condition at AC: TIR occurs when sin 45 >= 1/n, i.e. n >= 1/sin 45 = 2 = 1.414 → Compare each colour's refractive index (1.39, 1.44, 1.47) with 1.414 to decide which colours emerge through AC and which are totally reflected
            whyThe work is reading the 45-degree incidence angle at the hypotenuse from the figure, converting it to a critical refractive index of 2, and comparing the three given indices against that threshold.
            the catchOption 3 rewards the plausible wrong route of treating the prism as a dispersing prism; the question is actually about total internal reflection at the hypotenuse.
